claim: Decisions about noisy stimuli are widely understood to be made by accumulating evidence up to a decision bound that can be adjusted according to task demands.
source: Decisions about noisy stimuli are widely understood to be made by accumulating evidence up to a decision bound that can be adjusted according to task demands.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: Participants were faster in the mixed context than the fixed contexts.
source: Additionally, participants were faster in the mixed context than the fixed ones (main effect of difficulty context on RT in rANOVA, F(1, 13)=21.3, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows significant main effect of difficulty context on RT (F(1, 13)=21.3, p<0.001).

claim: A leaky accumulator model with a higher bound for the strong context was able to accurately reproduce behavioural data.
source: Confirming this, a leaky accumulator model with a higher bound for the strong context (Figure 1D and Table 1 for all the fitted parameters) was able to accurately reproduce behavioural data, particularly the important context-dependent false alarm pattern (see bars of the false alarm plot in Figure 1B; G2=16).
evidence: Model fitting results show good fit to behavioral data (G2=16), with reference to Figure 1D and Table 1.

claim: Beta oscillatory activity over motor cortical EEG sites gradually decreases in amplitude as participants prepare to make a movement with their contralateral limb.
source: It has long been established that beta oscillatory activity over motor cortical EEG sites gradually decreases in amplitude as participants prepare to make a movement with their contralateral limb (Donoghue et al., 1998; Pfurtscheller et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature (Donoghue et al., 1998; Pfurtscheller et al., 1996).

claim: Beta-indexed motor preparation signal builds at an evidence-dependent rate during decision formation and reaches a stereotyped threshold level at the time of motor execution.
source: First, it builds at an evidence-dependent rate during decision formation and reaches a stereotyped threshold level at the time of motor execution (Kelly et al., 2021; O'Connell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research (Kelly et al., 2021; O'Connell et al., 2012).

claim: Fluctuations in pre-target beta activity predict trial-to-trial behavioural variability in the way accumulator starting point variability does in models.
source: Second, fluctuations in pre-target beta activity have been shown to predict trial-to-trial behavioural variability in the way accumulator starting point variability does in models (de Lange et al., 2013; Donner et al., 2009; Gould et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research (de Lange et al., 2013; Donner et al., 2009; Gould et al., 2012).

claim: Pre-target beta is systematically shifted closer to its pre-response threshold level under conditions of speed emphasis.
source: Third, pre-target beta is systematically shifted closer to its pre-response threshold level under conditions of speed emphasis (Murphy et al., 2016; Steinemann et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research (Murphy et al., 2016; Steinemann et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2021).

claim: The beta amplitude prior to a false alarm closely matched the amplitude reached prior to a true target detection.
source: Additionally, we found that the beta amplitude prior to a false alarm closely matched to the amplitude reached prior a true target detection, verifying the assumption that this threshold level is applied consistently within each block (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Empirical observation from EEG data, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The CPP reflects pure cumulative evidence which feeds into motor-level decision variable alongside other evidence-independent signal components such as urgency.
source: The current working hypothesis is thus that the CPP reflects pure cumulative evidence which feeds into motor-level decision variable alongside other evidence-independent signal components such as urgency.
evidence: This is stated as a working hypothesis based on previous research.

claim: Simulations of pure cumulative evidence build-up have been shown to match empirical CPP waveforms in their dynamics and pre-response amplitude patterns across conditions and RTs.
source: In support of this scheme, simulations of pure cumulative evidence build-up have been shown to match empirical CPP waveforms in their dynamics and pre-response amplitude patterns across conditions and RTs (Afacan-Seref et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2021; Twomey et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research (Afacan-Seref et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2021; Twomey et al., 2015).

claim: Beta waveforms during the full ITIs showed that in addition to the static shift towards the motor execution threshold in the strong context, there was a strong tendency for beta to decrease over the course of the ITI in all contexts.
source: Beta waveforms during the full ITIs showed that in addition to the static shift towards the motor execution threshold in the strong context, there was a strong tendency for beta to decrease over the course of the ITI in all contexts (Figure 3A, lower).
evidence: Empirical observation from EEG data, with reference to Figure 3A, lower.

claim: The increasing trend in beta mirrored a tendency for false alarm rate to increase during the ITI.
source: This increasing trend in beta mirrored a tendency for false alarm rate to increase during the ITI (Figure 3A, upper).
evidence: Empirical observation from behavioral and EEG data, with reference to Figure 3A, upper.

claim: Both neurally informed models mimic the behavioural patterns well.
source: While both neurally informed models mimic the behavioural patterns well (see Figure 3B and C, goodness-of-fit in Table 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2), the leak-adjustment model provides a poorer fit (G2=23) to the behavioural data than the criterion-adjustment model (G2=16; see Figure 3B, lower).
evidence: Model fitting results show goodness-of-fit metrics (G2=23 and G2=16), with reference to Figure 3B, C and Table 1.

claim: The leak-adjustment model provides a poorer fit (G2=23) to the behavioural data than the criterion-adjustment model (G2=16).
source: While both neurally informed models mimic the behavioural patterns well (see Figure 3B and C, goodness-of-fit in Table 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2), the leak-adjustment model provides a poorer fit (G2=23) to the behavioural data than the criterion-adjustment model (G2=16; see Figure 3B, lower).
evidence: Model fitting results show goodness-of-fit metrics (G2=23 vs G2=16), with reference to Figure 3B, lower.

claim: Despite being constrained to adopt the precise bound settings indexed by beta excursion, the criterion-adjustment model was able to attain the same goodness-of-fit to behaviour as the initial bound-adjustment model (G2=16).
source: Remarkably, despite being constrained to adopt the precise bound settings indexed by beta excursion, which oppose the adjustments predicted by the bound-adjustment model, the criterion-adjustment model was able to attain the same goodness-of-fit to behaviour as the initial bound-adjustment model (G2=16).
evidence: Model fitting results show equal goodness-of-fit metrics (G2=16 for both models).

claim: The behavioural fits still favoured the criterion-adjustment model (G2+penalty = 24) over the leak-adjustment model (G2+penalty = 33) in the revised model fitting procedure.
source: The behavioural fits still favoured the criterion-adjustment model (G2+penalty = 24) over the leak-adjustment model (G2+penalty = 33; see Table 2), and as expected, estimated even larger urgency offsets to compensate for the asymptotic evidence accumulation levels.
evidence: Model fitting results show goodness-of-fit metrics (G2+penalty = 24 vs 33), with reference to Table 2.

claim: The empirical CPP slope time course plateaued in the strong conditions indicating a linear build-up profile.
source: We found that the empirical CPP slope time course plateaued in the strong conditions indicating a linear build-up profile (Figure 4A), whereas the simulated time course of the leaky accumulator models indeed showed a steep drop-off in temporal slope after an initial peak (Figure 4B/C).
evidence: Empirical observation from EEG data analysis, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The simulated time course of the leaky accumulator models showed a steep drop-off in temporal slope after an initial peak.
source: We found that the empirical CPP slope time course plateaued in the strong conditions indicating a linear build-up profile (Figure 4A), whereas the simulated time course of the leaky accumulator models indeed showed a steep drop-off in temporal slope after an initial peak (Figure 4B/C).
evidence: Model simulation results, with reference to Figure 4B/C.

claim: The criterion-adjustment model with non-leaky accumulation showed a plateau in the slope similar to the empirical CPP.
source: Meanwhile, the criterion-adjustment model with non-leaky accumulation showed a plateau in the slope similar to the empirical CPP (Figure 4D).
evidence: Model simulation results, with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: For the fixed strong condition the empirical slope dropped by 5% (bootstrap CI95% = [–5% 16%]).
source: For the fixed strong condition the empirical slope dropped by 5% (bootstrap CI95% = [–5% 16%]), while the criterion-adjustment model predicted a drop of 6%, and the leak-adjustment model a drop of 27.5%, the latter falling outside the empirical bootstrapped 95% CI.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of CPP slope with bootstrap confidence intervals.

claim: The criterion-adjustment model predicted a drop of 6% in slope for the fixed strong condition.
source: For the fixed strong condition the empirical slope dropped by 5% (bootstrap CI95% = [–5% 16%]), while the criterion-adjustment model predicted a drop of 6%, and the leak-adjustment model a drop of 27.5%, the latter falling outside the empirical bootstrapped 95% CI.
evidence: Model simulation results compared to empirical data.

claim: The leak-adjustment model predicted a drop of 27.5% in slope for the fixed strong condition, falling outside the empirical bootstrapped 95% CI.
source: For the fixed strong condition the empirical slope dropped by 5% (bootstrap CI95% = [–5% 16%]), while the criterion-adjustment model predicted a drop of 6%, and the leak-adjustment model a drop of 27.5%, the latter falling outside the empirical bootstrapped 95% CI.
evidence: Model simulation results compared to empirical data with statistical confidence intervals.

claim: In the mixed strong condition the empirical slope dropped by 1.5% (bootstrap CI95% = [–9.5% 13%]).
source: Similarly, in the mixed strong condition the empirical slope dropped by 1.5% (bootstrap CI95% = [–9.5% 13%]), compared to 3% predicted by the criterion-adjustment model and 17% predicted by the leak-adjustment model.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of CPP slope with bootstrap confidence intervals.

claim: The criterion-adjustment model predicted a drop of 3% in slope for the mixed strong condition.
source: Similarly, in the mixed strong condition the empirical slope dropped by 1.5% (bootstrap CI95% = [–9.5% 13%]), compared to 3% predicted by the criterion-adjustment model and 17% predicted by the leak-adjustment model.
evidence: Model simulation results compared to empirical data.

claim: The leak-adjustment model predicted a drop of 17% in slope for the mixed strong condition.
source: Similarly, in the mixed strong condition the empirical slope dropped by 1.5% (bootstrap CI95% = [–9.5% 13%]), compared to 3% predicted by the criterion-adjustment model and 17% predicted by the leak-adjustment model.
evidence: Model simulation results compared to empirical data.

claim: Fourteen participants were recruited at University College Dublin.
source: Fourteen participants (aged 21–60 years; eight female) were recruited at University College Dublin.
evidence: Direct statement of participant recruitment details.

claim: Two participants were left-handed.
source: Two participants were left-handed, all participants had normal or corrected-to-normal visual acuity, and had no previously diagnosed psychiatric disorders, epilepsy or suffered from any head injury resulting in loss of consciousness.
evidence: Direct statement of participant characteristics.

claim: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal visual acuity.
source: Two participants were left-handed, all participants had normal or corrected-to-normal visual acuity, and had no previously diagnosed psychiatric disorders, epilepsy or suffered from any head injury resulting in loss of consciousness.
evidence: Direct statement of participant characteristics.

claim: The UCD Human Research Ethics Committee for Life Sciences approved all experimental procedures in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
source: The UCD Human Research Ethics Committee for Life Sciences approved all experimental procedures in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (LS-16-76-Craddock).
evidence: Direct statement of ethical approval.

claim: Participants performed the task in a dark room, while seated 57 cm from the monitor.
source: Participants performed the task in a dark room, while seated 57 cm from the monitor.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental setup.

claim: All stimuli were presented on a black background on a 21-inch CRT monitor operating at 60 Hz refresh rate (1280×960 pixels).
source: All stimuli were presented on a black background on a 21-inch CRT monitor operating at 60 Hz refresh rate (1280×960 pixels).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental setup.

claim: Participants performed 12 blocks each consisting of 24 targets.
source: Each participant performed 12 blocks each consisting of 24 targets.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design.

claim: Three blocks of each of the 'fixed' contexts ('strong' or 'weak') were first run in an order counterbalanced across participants.
source: Three blocks of each of the 'fixed' (single-coherence targets) contexts ('strong' or 'weak') were first run in an order counterbalanced across participants.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design.

claim: All participants performed six 'mixed' blocks at the end of the experimental session.
source: The 'mixed' target coherence context was originally designed as a control condition to verify bound invariance across target strengths within a single context, and thus all participants performed six 'mixed' blocks at the end of the experimental session.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design.

claim: Continuous EEG was recorded from 128 scalp electrodes using a BioSemi system with a sample rate of 512 Hz.
source: Continuous EEG was recorded from 128 scalp electrodes using a BioSemi system with a sample rate of 512 Hz.
evidence: Direct statement of EEG recording parameters.

claim: One participant was excluded due to excessive trial rejection (>70% in each condition) due to a mix of blinking, eye movements, and EEG artefacts.
source: One participant was excluded due to excessive trial rejection (>70% in each condition) due to a mix of blinking, eye movements, and EEG artefacts.
evidence: Direct statement of data exclusion criteria and results.

claim: Motor preparation was measured via effector-selective spectral amplitude decreases in the beta (15–30 Hz) frequency range.
source: First, motor preparation was measured via effector-selective spectral amplitude decreases in the beta (15–30 Hz) frequency range.
evidence: Direct statement of analysis method.

claim: The CPP is a motor-independent signal exhibiting evidence accumulation dynamics.
source: Second, we analysed the CPP, a motor-independent signal exhibiting evidence accumulation dynamics (O'Connell et al., 2012; Kelly and O'Connell, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research (O'Connell et al., 2012; Kelly and O'Connell, 2013).

claim: The sensory criterion adjustment mechanism presents an alternative means of policy setting with respect to the strategic adjustment of the action-triggering bound.
source: The sensory criterion adjustment mechanism presents an interesting alternative means of policy setting with respect to the strategic adjustment of the action-triggering bound suggested by the dominant computational models and empirical research on the speed-accuracy trade-off (Bogacz et al., 2010; Palmer et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the study's findings, with reference to previous research (Bogacz et al., 2010; Palmer et al., 2005).

claim: When adjusting for expected difficulty level during continuous detection, people regulate the transfer of sensory evidence into the accumulator process rather than changing the decision bound.
source: In conclusion, while previous studies of decision policy adjustments for other perceptual task manipulations have found that they are enacted by changing the decision bound, we here show that, when adjusting for expected difficulty level during continuous detection, people instead regulate the transfer of sensory evidence into the accumulator process.
evidence: This is stated as the main conclusion of the study based on the empirical findings and model comparisons.

claim: The brain harbours a broader range of mechanisms to regulate decision policy than it had previously seemed.
source: This suggests that the brain harbours a broader range of mechanisms to regulate decision policy than it had previously seemed.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the study's findings.

claim: In continuous detection where target onsets are unpredictable, the decision process must operate continuously.
source: However, in continuous detection where target onsets are unpredictable, the decision process must operate continuously, offering other parameters that could alternatively be adjusted.
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference about the nature of continuous detection tasks.

claim: If accumulation proceeds continuously it is unlikely to be perfect because this generates excessive false alarms.
source: For example, if accumulation proceeds continuously it is unlikely to be perfect because this generates excessive false alarms (Ossmy et al., 2013) and would instead entail some form of information loss such as through non-linear or leaky accumulation, which has been shown to form a critical adjustable component governing decision-making policies in volatile environments (for review, see Gold and Stocker, 2017; Glaze et al., 2015; Harun et al., 2020; Murphy et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research (Ossmy et al., 2013; Gold and Stocker, 2017; Glaze et al., 2015; Harun et al., 2020; Murphy et al., 2021).

claim: Leaky accumulation has been shown to form a critical adjustable component governing decision-making policies in volatile environments.
source: For example, if accumulation proceeds continuously it is unlikely to be perfect because this generates excessive false alarms (Ossmy et al., 2013) and would instead entail some form of information loss such as through non-linear or leaky accumulation, which has been shown to form a critical adjustable component governing decision-making policies in volatile environments (for review, see Gold and Stocker, 2017; Glaze et al., 2015; Harun et al., 2020; Murphy et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research (Gold and Stocker, 2017; Glaze et al., 2015; Harun et al., 2020; Murphy et al., 2021).

claim: Motor-selective cortical networks implement an increase of baseline activity prior to evidence onset to emphasize speed by effectively decreasing the criterion amount of cumulative evidence needed to reach an action-triggering threshold.
source: In these studies, motor-selective cortical networks have been shown to implement an increase of baseline activity prior to evidence onset, emphasising speed by effectively decreasing the criterion amount of cumulative evidence needed to reach an action-triggering threshold (Forstmann et al., 2008; Forstmann et al., 2010; Ivanoff et al., 2008; van Veen et al., 2008; Wenzlaff et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research (Forstmann et al., 2008; Forstmann et al., 2010; Ivanoff et al., 2008; van Veen et al., 2008; Wenzlaff et al., 2011).

claim: Recent behavioural and neurophysiological findings have established the operation of a time-dependent 'urgency' signal in motor circuits.
source: Additionally, recent behavioural and neurophysiological findings have established the operation of a time-dependent 'urgency' signal in these motor circuits, an evidence-independent build-up component that drives the decision process closer to a fixed decision threshold, gradually decreasing the cumulative evidence required to respond (Churchland et al., 2008; Hanks et al., 2014; Murphy et al., 2016; Thura and Cisek, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research (Churchland et al., 2008; Hanks et al., 2014; Murphy et al., 2016; Thura and Cisek, 2016).

claim: An urgency signal is an evidence-independent build-up component that drives the decision process closer to a fixed decision threshold, gradually decreasing the cumulative evidence required to respond.
source: Additionally, recent behavioural and neurophysiological findings have established the operation of a time-dependent 'urgency' signal in these motor circuits, an evidence-independent build-up component that drives the decision process closer to a fixed decision threshold, gradually decreasing the cumulative evidence required to respond (Churchland et al., 2008; Hanks et al., 2014; Murphy et al., 2016; Thura and Cisek, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research (Churchland et al., 2008; Hanks et al., 2014; Murphy et al., 2016; Thura and Cisek, 2016).

claim: In continuous detection contexts containing weaker targets, contexts call for a more liberal decision policy.
source: In such contexts, expected target strength is a key factor in setting a decision policy to optimise performance – contexts with weaker targets call for a more liberal decision policy.
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference about optimal decision policy.

claim: An overly liberal policy could result in an excessive amount of false alarms driven solely by noise in between targets.
source: Here, an overly liberal policy could result in an excessive amount of false alarms driven solely by noise in between targets, while an overly conservative policy will miss too many targets (Gold and Stocker, 2017; Ossmy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference with support from citations (Gold and Stocker, 2017; Ossmy et al., 2013).

claim: An overly conservative policy will miss too many targets.
source: Here, an overly liberal policy could result in an excessive amount of false alarms driven solely by noise in between targets, while an overly conservative policy will miss too many targets (Gold and Stocker, 2017; Ossmy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference with support from citations (Gold and Stocker, 2017; Ossmy et al., 2013).
